idiom_name: Semaphore[F] with acquire / release and permit.use
implementation_notes: In effect-oriented Scala the realization is cats.effect.std.Semaphore[F]: acquire and release are IO values, acquisition fiber-blocks (semantic blocking without pinning a thread) and is cancelable, Semaphore[F](n) is the constructor, and s.permit.use(...) brackets acquisition and release so the permit is returned on success, error and cancellation alike. It is fair and cancellation-safe; choose it when the program is written in IO, and keep the JVM semaphore for blocking interop or Future-based code.
pitfalls: Semaphore[F] must be constructed inside the effect (Semaphore[IO](8)) rather than captured at object-initialisation time, or the effect is not referentially transparent.
A blocking java.util.concurrent.Semaphore acquired inside an IO fiber pins a compute thread; use the effectful semaphore or wrap blocking calls in IO.blocking.
Manual acquire without a finalizer leaks permits when the fiber is cancelled; prefer permit.use, which brackets the acquisition.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent.Semaphore (JVM blocking)
variants.implementation_notes: Scala compiles to the JVM, so java.util.concurrent.Semaphore is always available without any dependency: acquire()/tryAcquire(timeout, unit)/release(n) with an optional fairness flag, usable directly from Scala code. It is the right choice for blocking interop - executor tasks, Future callbacks, JNI, legacy libraries - and the wrong one inside an IO/fs2 fiber, where it would occupy a compute thread while waiting.
pitfalls: release() has no upper bound; over-release silently raises the permit count above the constructor value.
acquire() is uninterruptible unless you use acquireInterruptibly, so cancellation from a fiber cannot break the wait.
The JUC semaphore and cats-effect's Semaphore are different counters; using both for one resource gives two bounds that cannot be reasoned about together.
